He is Robin Goodfellow, the trickster called Puck, placed at Meghan's side long ago by a master he will not name, and he agrees, reluctantly, to take her across into the Nevernever to get her brother back.

Puck leads Meghan into the Nevernever, the fey world shaped by human belief, and drills her in its rules: never give a fey your true name, never eat its food, never accept anything without first agreeing the price. They are hunted almost at once, dodge the Wild Hunt, and acquire a travelling companion in Grimalkin, a talking grey cat who trades guidance for a favour to be collected later. Meghan then learns that she was never entirely human. Puck's master is Oberon, the Erlking of the Summer Court, and Meghan is his daughter by a mortal woman, a half-blood princess of Summer, which is why the fey have always noticed her. Brought before the Seelie Court, she is acknowledged by a father who is courteous, remote and unwilling to send his court after Ethan, and detested on sight by Titania, Oberon's queen, to whom Meghan is living proof of her husband's infidelity. Whatever took Ethan, the Summer Court will not name it.

Titania makes the Summer Court unsafe for Meghan, and Oberon's protection amounts to keeping his daughter where he can see her rather than helping her search. At Elysium, the truce gathering where Summer and Winter meet without bloodshed, Meghan meets Ash, the youngest son of Mab of the Winter Court, a prince who hunts for his mother and would like nothing better than to bring Oberon's half-human daughter home to her. Out of options, Meghan makes a bargain with him: he will help her find and recover Ethan, and when it is done she will go with him to the Winter Court as Mab's. With Grimalkin's help she gets out of the Seelie Court and away from Titania, and the search finally begins on terms of her own.

Meghan's search takes her back across the Nevernever, where the wyldwood is sickening in patches: trees rusting, glamour failing, whole groves dying in ways nothing in Faery will discuss. Puck rejoins her, and the answer arrives with the creatures that keep attacking her. There is a new kind of fey in the world, born not of the old stories but of what humans believe in now, machines and wires and progress, and the iron in them is lethal to every traditional fey. The courts refuse to acknowledge that the Iron fey exist, because admitting it would mean admitting the old fey are being killed by the very thing that once made them. It was the Iron fey who took Ethan, on the orders of their king, Machina, the figure Meghan glimpsed in her computer screen and Ethan saw in his closet.

To find Machina's realm Meghan has to leave the Nevernever and go looking in the mortal world. In New Orleans she seeks out the Oracle, a fey seer in the shape of an old woman who deals in what is coming and sets her own terms for it. The price is steep and Meghan pays it. The Iron fey track her through the city, proving that the wyldwood, the mortal world and even a dryad's hold in a public park are all now within their reach, and the attacks come closer together. Meghan also begins to work out what she can do herself: she is Oberon's daughter, carrying Summer glamour she barely knows how to hold, and her human half lets her handle iron that would burn a full-blooded fey to the bone.

Meghan, Ash, Puck and Grimalkin cross into the Iron Realm, a country of slag, scrap and poisoned air where Ash and Puck weaken with every hour they remain. They bargain passage from packrats, evade iron dragons, and are hunted first by Ironhorse, one of Machina's lieutenants, and then by the Iron King's armoured knights. There is no way through for all of them. Ash turns and holds the knights off so that Meghan can reach Machina's tower, and she goes on without him, knowing what it is likely to cost him.

Meghan reaches the heart of the Iron Realm and finds Ethan alive and wired into Machina's machinery, being used to feed the Iron King's power. Machina does not attack her; he explains himself. He is dying and his realm is dying with him, and he wants Meghan, Oberon's daughter, untouched by iron, able to carry Summer glamour and iron glamour alike, to take a place at his side and sustain what he built. She refuses, turns her own power on him and destroys him, but he goes out unafraid: the Iron fey are made by human belief, belief has not stopped, and his crown will not stay empty. Meghan frees Ethan, brings him home, and returns him to a family who will never learn where he was. Her reprieve is short. Ash arrives to collect on the bargain she made at Elysium, and Meghan leaves with him for the Winter Court.

characters.description: The narrator of this book: the youngest son of Mab, exiled from the Winter Court and now sworn knight to the Iron Queen, who ordered him out of her realm because its iron was killing him. He is precise, formal and extremely dangerous, has spent centuries as his mother's weapon, and keeps what any of it cost him strictly to himself. He has set out to acquire the one thing no fey possesses, a mortal soul, because without it he cannot stand where Meghan now has to stay.
characters.name: Ash

characters.description: The trickster, Oberon's servant, who invites himself along on a journey he was not asked to join and jokes his way through every part of it. He and Ash have a blood feud Ash swore long ago to settle in a killing, and both of them know that the only reason it is still unsettled is Meghan.
characters.name: Puck

characters.description: The cait sith, who turns up as a guide at his own price and disappears the moment a situation becomes tedious or lethal. He knows where the party is going and rather more about why than he is prepared to say.
characters.name: Grimalkin

characters.description: Oberon's half-human daughter, now Queen of the Iron Realm, which she took the crown of to stop it destroying Faery. Ash swore himself to her as her knight and cannot reach her: the iron of her realm would kill any ordinary fey, and she used her authority as his queen to send him out of it.
characters.name: Meghan Chase

characters.description: Queen of the Winter Court and Ash's mother, who cast him out for putting Oberon's daughter above his own court. She raised her sons as instruments of Winter and has never forgiven one of them for choosing anything else.
characters.name: Mab

characters.description: An enormous grey fey grown out of every retelling of the wolf in human stories, who attaches himself to the party uninvited. He is entirely honest about being a predator and about having reasons of his own for wanting to see how this journey ends.
characters.name: The Wolf

characters.description: A girl of the Winter Court who was Ash's first love and who died years ago on a hunt Ash has blamed Puck for ever since. She appears on the road alive and unchanged, joins the journey, and says only that she was taken out of her death and kept away from the world for a reason she is not ready to explain.
characters.name: Ariella

characters.description: The keeper of the trials at the far end of the world, an ancient thing that decides whether a fey may be given a mortal soul and sets the tests that settle the question. It is neither cruel nor merciful; it simply requires that anyone asking be shown exactly what he already is.
characters.name: The Guardian

recaps.ending: Ash passes the Guardian's trials at the end of the world, the last of them a temptation rather than a fight: an entire life in which Ariella never died and Meghan has no part in it, which he refuses. The soul he is asking for requires a life given in exchange, and Ariella gives hers, telling him she had already seen it and was kept alive for no other purpose. Ash is remade with a mortal soul, still himself but finite and vulnerable, and no longer destroyed by iron. The blood feud between Ash and Puck, which began with Ariella's first death and which Ash had sworn to end in a killing, is closed by her second; the two part alive and no longer sworn enemies, on terms neither of them says out loud. Grimalkin departs with his favours uncollected, as he generally does. Ash leaves the end of the world, crosses the border that would have killed him before, and reaches the Iron Realm and Meghan's court, where he can now stay. The original quartet closes with Meghan established as the Iron Queen and Ash beside her, the Iron Realm accepted as a third power in Faery, and Meghan's human family left behind in the mortal world.
recaps.in_short: Told from Ash's point of view. Exiled from Winter and ordered out of the Iron Realm by Meghan so that its iron would not kill him, Ash sets out to gain a mortal soul, the one thing that would let him live at her side. Puck comes along uninvited, Grimalkin guides them at his usual price, and the Big Bad Wolf follows for reasons of his own. On the road they are joined by Ariella, Ash's first love, whose death long ago began his feud with Puck, alive and unwilling to explain how. They reach the end of the world, where a Guardian sets the trials that decide whether a fey may be given a soul. Ash is made to face everything he has done as Mab's weapon, and is finally offered an entire happy life in which Ariella never died and Meghan does not exist. He refuses it. The price of the soul is a life, and Ariella gives hers, saying she was kept alive for exactly this. Ash is remade with a mortal soul, no longer vulnerable to iron, his feud with Puck ended rather than settled. He crosses into the Iron Realm and reaches Meghan for good.

recaps.text: Previously, and told this time from Ash's point of view. Meghan Chase, the half-human daughter of Oberon of the Summer Court, was drawn into Faery when Iron fey, a new breed born of human belief in machines and lethal to ordinary fey, stole her little brother. She destroyed their king Machina, was held afterwards in the Winter Court under a bargain with Ash, Mab's youngest son, and fell in love with him. When Iron fey stole the Scepter of the Seasons and set the courts at war, Meghan recovered it and stopped the fighting by wielding iron glamour openly; Oberon banished her for it, and Ash was cast out of Winter for choosing her. In exile the two of them were sent back into the Iron Realm to kill the usurper wearing Machina's crown. Meghan killed him, and then, because the realm's power had to be held by someone or it would go on devouring Faery and she was the only one who could hold it, she took the crown herself and became the Iron Queen. That bound her to a realm whose iron kills any ordinary fey. Ash, her sworn knight and already dying of the exposure, was ordered out of her territory by his own queen so that he would live. Meghan gave up her human family and her mortal life along with him. Ash left the Iron Realm alive, exiled from Winter, unable to return to the one person he wants, and determined to change that.

Ash's answer is the one thing no fey has: a mortal soul. With one he could survive the Iron Realm and stand beside Meghan; without one he cannot cross her borders and live. The difficulty is that nobody in Faery can tell him it has ever been done. Puck invites himself along, which Ash tolerates because Puck is useful and because the blood feud between them, sworn over Ariella's death long ago, is a debt neither of them intends to settle while Meghan needs them both alive. Grimalkin turns up to guide them at his usual price. They travel out into the deep wyldwood, far past any territory the courts hold, and acquire an unwanted companion in the Big Bad Wolf, an enormous fey made out of every retelling of the story, who is entirely honest about being a predator and about wanting to see how Ash's journey ends.

The road runs through country with no interest in whether they survive it, and the answers they collect are consistent: what Ash wants can be granted only at the end of the world, by a guardian who sets trials, and the price is something nobody will name in advance. A hooded stranger joins the party, and she is not a stranger. Ariella, the Winter girl Ash loved and watched die years ago, the death he has blamed Puck for ever since, is alive, unchanged and travelling with them. She says she was taken out of her death and kept away from the world for a reason she is not yet willing to give. Her presence takes apart the one certainty Ash's last several centuries have been built on, and it puts Puck in an impossible position.

The party crosses out of the known world entirely, past anything mapped, and reaches the place where the trials are held. The Guardian there is neither hostile nor kind: it simply requires that a fey asking to be given a soul be shown, precisely, what he already is. The tests begin with Ash's own history. He has been Mab's son and Mab's weapon for a very long time and has killed a great many people in that service, and the trials make him meet what he did rather than remember it from a distance. There is no version of the account in which he was not responsible.

The trials continue past the point where Ash's companions can follow him. The last of them is not a fight but an offer: an entire life in which Ariella never died, in which the hunt went differently and the centuries since were happy ones. It is convincing, it costs nothing to accept, and accepting it means Meghan is not in it. Ash refuses and comes out the other side, which the Guardian treats as the answer it was looking for. What remains is the price, and by this point it is clear that the price is a life.

The soul cannot be granted without a life given for it, and Ariella gives hers. She tells Ash she was kept alive precisely for this, that she had already seen it and came back for no other reason, and she goes willingly and over his objection. Ash is remade: he keeps himself, but with a mortal soul and a mortal's vulnerability, and iron can no longer destroy him. Whatever lies between him and Puck over Ariella is not repaid, but it is finished, and the feud ends without a killing. Ash leaves the end of the world, crosses into the Iron Realm that would have killed him before, and walks into Meghan's court to stay. The quartet closes with the two of them together in the realm she gave up everything else to hold.

characters.description: Oberon's half-human daughter, banished from the Nevernever and living rough in the mortal world with Ash. She has stopped being able to pretend she is an ordinary girl: she carries Summer glamour and can also touch iron glamour, the power lethal to every other fey, which is precisely why the courts threw her out. She wants to get home and see her family before she decides what her life is now.
characters.name: Meghan Chase

characters.description: The youngest son of Mab, cast out of the Winter Court for choosing Meghan over his queen and his family. He travels the mortal world with her, guards her without being asked, and treats exile as the price of a decision he has no intention of regretting.
characters.name: Ash

characters.description: The trickster who guarded Meghan for years disguised as a schoolboy and has fought beside her ever since. He serves Oberon, jokes through anything lethal, is in love with Meghan and has never made a claim on it, and his long feud with Ash remains unsettled.
characters.name: Puck

characters.description: The cait sith who has guided Meghan through every crisis so far, on credit. He talks, vanishes at will, knows far more than he admits, and collects the favours he is owed at moments of his own choosing.
characters.name: Grimalkin

characters.description: Meghan's young half brother, living in Louisiana with their mother and stepfather. He was stolen by the Iron fey once already and got back a sister who then vanished out of his life for months at a time.
characters.name: Ethan Chase

characters.description: The Erlking, ruler of the Summer Court and Meghan's father, who banished her from the Nevernever after she used iron glamour in front of both courts. He calls it protection; it is also a court removing a danger it cannot control.
characters.name: Oberon

characters.description: Queen of the Winter Court, who exiled her own youngest son for choosing Oberon's daughter over Tir Na Nog. She has lost a son to the Iron fey, another to treachery and a third to Meghan, and she has forgiven none of it.
characters.name: Mab

characters.description: Queen of the Summer Court, Oberon's wife, who has wanted Meghan gone since the day she learned of her existence and regards the banishment as overdue.
characters.name: Titania

characters.description: An Iron fey lieutenant with hair like arcing lightning, once one of the old Iron King's officers and now the leader of a resistance among the Iron fey themselves. His people refuse to serve the king who took Machina's crown, and he seeks Meghan out because he believes the crown was never that king's to take.
characters.name: Glitch

characters.description: The Iron fey's new ruler, who claimed Machina's crown after his death and whose realm is spreading into the Nevernever far faster than his predecessor's ever did. The Iron rebels call him a usurper and a false king; the old courts, still refusing to admit that the Iron fey exist at all, are running out of ground on which to deny him.
characters.name: The False King

characters.description: Mab's son, exposed in the war over the Scepter of the Seasons as the traitor who sold Winter to the Iron fey. He never came back to his mother's court, and Meghan's party finds him still in Iron service when they cross into the realm.
characters.name: Rowan

characters.description: A gremlin of the Iron Realm, small, wire-thin and all teeth, who takes an immediate liking to Meghan's party and refuses to be left behind. He speaks in fragments, chews through anything mechanical within reach, and is destructive without meaning any harm by it.
characters.name: Razor

characters.description: The Iron Realm's first king, who ruled before Machina took the crown from him. He did not die when he lost the throne, and the long years since have left him with a considerable grievance and a great deal of knowledge about how the crown actually works.
characters.name: Ferrum

recaps.ending: Meghan destroys the false Iron King in the battle for Faery, and then makes the choice the whole book has been driving toward. The Iron Realm's power has to be held by someone or it will go on consuming the Nevernever, and she is the only creature alive who can hold it without being destroyed by it. She takes the crown and becomes the Iron Queen, which means remaining in a realm no unaltered fey can enter and survive. That includes Ash, who is already dying of iron exposure and refuses to leave her, so Meghan uses the one authority he cannot argue with: she is his queen and he is her sworn knight, and she orders him out of her territory, releasing him from her service rather than watch him die in it. She also loses the human life she had spent three books trying to get back to, leaving her mother, her stepfather and Ethan behind for good. The war with the Iron fey ends, Faery survives, and Meghan becomes a third monarch the old courts have to acknowledge. Ash leaves the Iron Realm alive and entirely unwilling to accept the arrangement. In the closing pages he sets out to find a way to become something that can live in iron, by earning a mortal soul, which is the journey the next book follows.
recaps.in_short: Exiled from Faery, Meghan Chase and Ash are living in the mortal world when the Iron fey find them. The false king who took Machina's crown is expanding the Iron Realm far faster than his predecessor, and the iron creeping through the wyldwood is killing Faery outright. Glitch's Iron rebels want the usurper gone; Oberon and Mab want the same, and offer to lift Meghan's exile if she goes into the Iron Realm and kills him, since she is the only being who can survive there. Ash trains her to fight and then swears himself to her as her knight, Puck rejoins them, and Rowan turns up still serving the enemy. In the Iron Realm they learn the realm's history and how its crown passes, and Meghan works out what winning will actually cost. In the final battle she destroys the false king and then takes the loose Iron crown herself, becoming the Iron Queen, which binds her to a realm no ordinary fey can enter. She orders the dying Ash out of it to save his life and gives up her human family for good. Ash leaves vowing to find a way to earn a mortal soul and come back.

recaps.text: Previously: Meghan Chase discovered she was the half-human daughter of Oberon, king of the Summer Court, when Iron fey stole her little brother. She recovered him, destroyed their king Machina, and was warned as he died that the Iron crown would not stay empty. Paying the bargain that made the rescue possible, she went to the Winter Court as the hostage of Queen Mab, mother of Ash, the prince she had fallen in love with. Iron fey then ambushed the ceremony that passes the Scepter of the Seasons between the courts, killed one of Mab's sons and stole the Scepter; Winter blamed Summer and went to war. Meghan escaped to the mortal world, found Puck again, reached Leanansidhe the Exile Queen, in whose house she found her long-missing human father alive with his memory stripped, and with Puck, Ash, Grimalkin and the reformed Iron fey Ironhorse she stole the Scepter back. Ash's brother Rowan was exposed as the traitor working for the Iron fey, and Ironhorse died destroying the Iron fey Virus. Meghan stopped the war by returning the Scepter on the battlefield, but did it by openly wielding iron glamour, the power lethal to every other fey. Oberon banished her from the Nevernever, and Ash, who chose her over Winter, was exiled too. This book opens with the two of them in the mortal world with nowhere in Faery to go.

Exiled from the Nevernever, Meghan and Ash work their way through the mortal world toward Meghan's home in Louisiana, hunted along the road by things that should not be able to find an exile at all, including church grims and Iron fey scouts. Meghan wants to see her family before she works out what her life is now; what she learns instead is that banishment has not made her any less of a target. The Iron fey reach her first. Glitch, once an officer of the old Iron King and now the leader of a resistance among the Iron fey themselves, seeks her out. His people will not serve the king who took Machina's crown, whom they call a usurper, and they hold that the crown was never his to take. Glitch brings Meghan to a hidden sanctuary and puts an argument to her that she does not want to hear.

The false king's realm is expanding far faster than Machina's ever did, and the iron creeping into the wyldwood is killing Faery outright rather than merely poisoning it. Meghan decides to stop being someone who has to be rescued. Ash trains her to fight in earnest, and she works at both kinds of glamour she carries, the Summer power inherited from Oberon and the iron glamour no other fey can survive, let alone use. Puck catches up with them and the unresolved three-cornered tension between the three of them resumes where it left off. Ash then does something that cannot be undone: he swears himself to Meghan as her knight, a formal and binding oath of service and protection that puts her above his court, his exile and his own life.

Oberon and Mab summon the exiles they threw out. Faery is losing ground to the Iron Realm, and both monarchs have privately stopped pretending otherwise, though neither will say so where the other courts can hear it. Their offer is a bargain: Meghan is the only creature who can walk into the Iron Realm and survive, so she is to go and kill the false king, and in exchange her exile and Ash's will be lifted. It is not phrased as a request. Meghan agrees and sets out for the Iron Realm with Ash, Puck and Grimalkin, with Glitch's rebels for allies. On the way they meet the traitor knight, Rowan, Ash's own brother, who sold Winter to the Iron fey and is still serving them.

Inside the Iron Realm the party crosses country that is actively hostile to everything Ash and Puck are: the iron in the air weakens them by the hour, and Meghan can only slow it down. They pass through the ruins of Machina's old territory, left to rot since his death, and seek out a clockmaker who has survived every change of rule and knows more about the Iron crown than anyone living. A gremlin named Razor attaches himself to the party and cannot be shaken off. Meghan learns what the crown really is: not an ornament but the realm's power itself, held by whoever is strong enough to carry it, which is why the false king wears it and why Machina's death left it loose in the first place.

The realm's history comes out. Ferrum, the Iron Realm's first king, ruled before Machina deposed him, and he did not die when he lost the throne. Rowan puts a proposal of his own to Meghan. The fighting inside the realm becomes Iron against Iron as Glitch's rebels move openly against the king's forces. Meghan works out what killing the false king would actually require of her, and what it would cost afterwards, which is the part nobody who sent her has been willing to discuss. She and Ash spend the last night before the battle together, both of them aware that the bargain with Oberon and Mab contains no promise that she survives it.

The Iron fey advance on Faery and the courts of Summer and Winter meet them in open battle. Meghan reaches the false king and destroys him, and the Iron Realm's power, the crown itself, is left with nowhere to go. Left loose it will keep expanding and keep killing Faery, and Meghan is the only being who can take it and live. She takes it. Becoming the Iron Queen makes the Iron Realm her home and her responsibility: she cannot leave it, and nothing that is not iron-touched can survive inside it for long. That includes Ash, who is already failing from the exposure and will not leave voluntarily. Meghan uses the one authority he cannot refuse, ordering her sworn knight out of her realm to save his life. She also gives up the mortal life she had been fighting to get back to, and her family with it. The book ends with Meghan crowned in the Iron Realm and Ash outside it, released from her service and refusing to accept that the parting is permanent.

characters.description: A teenager living in a mountain settlement a year after solar flares scoured the planet. He survived the disaster as a boy in a flooded New York subway tunnel and walked out of the ruined city with the handful of people who got out with him. Practical, stubborn, and broken-sleeping from what he saw, he has built a rough life of chores, salvage and rationing around Trina, the girl he loves, and Alec, the old soldier whose planning keeps the settlement alive.
characters.name: Mark

characters.description: A girl Mark's age who sheltered in the same subway tunnel when the flares hit and has been beside him ever since. Warm, level-headed, and quicker than Mark to say plainly what she thinks, she is the reason he keeps to a routine at all, and the settlement leans on her steadiness as much as on Alec's discipline.
characters.name: Trina

characters.description: A former soldier decades older than Mark, who took command in the tunnels after the flares and led the survivors north out of the ruins. Blunt, hard-headed and relentlessly competent, he drills Mark, plans for the worst case, and has no patience for anything he considers sentiment. He is the closest thing the settlement has to a leader.
characters.name: Alec

characters.description: An army nurse who escaped the city alongside Alec and serves as the settlement's medic. Calm and unsentimental in a crisis, she is the person the sick and injured are brought to, and one of the few people willing to tell Alec when he is wrong.
characters.name: Lana

characters.description: A young man in Mark's circle of friends at the settlement, talkative and quick to joke, who shares the salvage runs and the daily work of keeping the place going.
characters.name: Darnell

characters.description: One of the young survivors who came out of the city with Mark's group and settled in the mountains with them, part of the small circle he spends his days with.
characters.name: Misty

characters.description: A boy in Mark's circle at the settlement, known by a nickname rather than a name, and one of the survivors of the walk out of the flooded city.
characters.name: Toad

characters.description: A man Mark and Alec find inside the fortified city of Asheville, hiding from both the infected and the authorities who sealed the place. He knows considerably more than an ordinary survivor about what the surviving governments have been doing about the sickness, and about what they intend to do to the region.
characters.name: Bruce

characters.description: A small girl the group encounters far from home, alone and hunted by people who blame her for what the sickness has done to their own families. She has not fallen ill, which is exactly why they want her dead. She says very little, gives her name as Deedee, and has survived conditions that have destroyed everyone around her.
characters.name: Deedee

recaps.ending: Mark's group reaches a landed Berg and gets Deedee, the immune girl, into the hands of people equipped to fly her out and study her, on the reasoning that the organization responsible for the virus is the only one left with the means to do anything useful with her. The bombardment of the infected region goes ahead on schedule. Alec does not survive it. Mark, whose own infection has been eating his memory and his self-control for days, finds Trina, who no longer reliably knows who he is, and stays with her rather than run; neither of them survives, and the settlement's remaining survivors are killed with them. The virus is not contained, cured, or explained away. Burning one region is an attempt to buy time, and the book is explicit that the disease is already well outside it. Deedee is flown out alone, told that her old life is finished and that she will be given a new name, and the name she is given is Teresa. That is the handoff to the rest of the series: the disease later known as the Flare is loose and incurable, immunity is the only asset anyone has, and the organization that will eventually run the Maze trials has just acquired its first immune child and a reason to believe her brain is worth taking apart.
recaps.in_short: A year after solar flares scorched the earth, Mark and a small group of survivors are scratching out a life in the Appalachian mountains when an aircraft appears over their settlement and fires darts down into the crowd. The darts carry an engineered virus that brings fever and then madness. Chasing the aircraft, Mark and the old soldier Alec learn that the disease was released deliberately as population control by the governments that survived the disaster, and that it has escaped every limit set for it. With their village destroyed and their friends turning violent, they head for the walled city of Asheville, only to find it quarantined and condemned: the whole region is to be firebombed. On the way out they take in Deedee, a small girl the disease cannot touch, and get her to the people who can make use of that. Mark, Trina and Alec, infected or trapped, die in the bombardment. Deedee is flown to safety and renamed Teresa.

recaps.text: The Kill Order stands apart from the Maze Runner trilogy. It is a prequel set roughly thirteen years before the events of The Maze Runner, and it follows an entirely new cast: ordinary survivors of the solar flares that wrecked the planet, not the Gladers. No knowledge of the trilogy is needed to follow it, and none of the trilogy's characters appear in the main story. What the book supplies is the origin of the world the trilogy inherits, namely how the disease at the center of that series was released, why so much of the population is infected, and how the organization the Gladers will later face got its start. The one direct connection to the later books is made at the edges of the novel, in the framing chapters that open and close it, rather than in the story itself. A reader new to the series can begin here; a reader who has finished the trilogy will recognize some of the machinery and terminology, but no plot point from those books is required to follow this one.

A year after the sun flares, Mark lives in a mountain settlement in the Appalachians with the people who escaped New York alongside him: Trina, the former soldier Alec, the nurse Lana, and friends including Darnell, Misty and Toad. Their days are chores, salvage and rationing, and Mark's nights are broken by memories of the disaster. That routine ends when an aircraft called a Berg drops low over the village, opens its hatch, and men in protective suits fire darts down into the crowd. Several villagers are hit, Darnell among them, and the Berg leaves as abruptly as it arrived. Nobody understands what the darts were meant to do, and within hours the first of the wounded is running a fever.

Darnell's fever turns quickly into confusion and then violence, and it becomes clear the darts carried something deliberate. Mark and Alec set out after the Berg and find it grounded not far from the settlement. They get aboard, fight through a crew that is itself coming apart, and take away documents and equipment before the craft goes down in the mountains. What they piece together is worse than an attack on one village: the darts carried an engineered virus released as policy by the governments that survived the flares, and their settlement was never supposed to be anywhere near its path. Interleaved through all of this are Mark's memories of the day the flares came, of the subway tunnel, the water that nearly drowned them, and the walk out of a burning city with Trina, Alec and Lana.

Mark and Alec return to a settlement that has turned on itself. The infection presents as fever first, then paranoia and rage, and neighbors the group has lived beside for a year attack them without warning. People die, the huts burn, and the survivors scatter. With nothing left in the mountains, the remnants of Mark's circle decide to make for Asheville, the nearest place said to still have walls, a functioning government and doctors. The journey is on foot through country the flares already emptied, and everyone they meet has to be assessed for signs of the sickness before it is safe to approach them.

The road to Asheville is a run of encounters with people at different stages of the disease: some feverish and frightened, some past reason and hunting anything that moves. The group loses members along the way. Mark's flashbacks fill in how they came to be here at all, from the tunnel that saved them and nearly killed them, through weeks of scavenging in the ruins, to Alec's decision to march everyone out to high ground and start again. By the time the mountains open onto the city the group is smaller and hungrier, and beginning to suspect that whatever was in the darts is already working inside some of them.

Asheville turns out to be sealed rather than saved: walled, patrolled, and quietly full of infected people the authorities have penned in rather than treated. Mark and Alec get inside and find Bruce, a man in hiding who supplies the rest of the picture. The virus was engineered and released deliberately as population control, on the reasoning that the flares left far more people than the ruined world could feed. It did not behave as designed. It spreads faster than intended, it mutates, and it destroys the mind rather than simply killing the body. The plan now on the table is to erase the whole infected region from the air, and everyone still inside it is included in that, sick or not.

Driven back out of the city ahead of the coming strike, the group comes across a small girl being hunted by villagers who blame her for their own sickness: she has not fallen ill, which is exactly why they want her dead. Mark and Alec take her with them. She barely speaks and gives her name only as Deedee. Her existence changes what the journey is for, because if the virus genuinely cannot touch her she is worth more to anyone still trying to solve it than the rest of them put together. Meanwhile the disease is working through the group itself. Trina's memory begins to slip, and there are stretches in which she does not recognize Mark at all.

Mark has to accept that he is infected as well. The fevers arrive with rages he cannot always account for afterward, and he begins measuring his decisions against how long he has before he is no use to anyone. Trina is further gone than he is. Alec, still functioning, works the problem the only way he knows how: find transport, get the immune girl to people with the equipment to study her, and do it before the region is burned. The group makes for a landed Berg, moving through country that is now openly hostile, with the strike aircraft already gathering overhead.

The last push is to put Deedee on an aircraft. Mark and Alec reach a Berg and hold it long enough for the girl to be handed to people equipped to take her out, the same organization whose policy caused all of this and the only one now capable of doing anything with an immune child. The others do not leave with her. The strike arrives as promised and the region is firebombed. Alec is killed, and Mark, his mind failing, finds Trina in the last minutes and stays with her instead of running; neither survives. Deedee is flown out alone. In the closing frame she is told she will be given a new life and a new name, and that name is Teresa, which is the point at which the book hands off directly to the world of the Maze Runner trilogy.

characters.description: A St. Louis animator and court-authorized vampire executioner. Anita begins the book engaged to Richard but still honoring an agreement to date Jean-Claude, and a professional contract on her life forces her to rely on both supernatural allies and the hunter Edward.
characters.name: Anita Blake

characters.description: A professional hunter and assassin known to vampires as Death. Edward warns Anita that someone has offered a large payment for her death and helps her identify and survive the specialists attempting to collect it.
characters.name: Edward

characters.description: Anita's fiancé, a junior-high science teacher, and one of the strongest werewolves in St. Louis. Richard wants to replace Marcus's coercive leadership but remains unwilling to embrace the killing expected by traditional pack law.
characters.name: Richard Zeeman

characters.description: The master vampire of St. Louis, linked to Anita through mystical marks and now formally competing with Richard for her affection. Jean-Claude offers guarded rooms and supernatural allies to protect Anita from the contract on her life.
characters.name: Jean-Claude

characters.description: A strong werewolf who joins the effort to protect Anita. Cassandra presents herself as practical and independent of the St. Louis pack's central rivalry, making her useful when Anita needs guards who understand shapeshifter threats.
characters.name: Cassandra

characters.description: An ancient master vampire whose body is deteriorating after a long refusal to take human blood. Sabin comes to St. Louis seeking a remedy from Anita and Jean-Claude before his effort to preserve his principles destroys him.
characters.name: Sabin

characters.description: Sabin's human servant and a necromancer with extensive knowledge of the bond between a vampire and a mortal partner. Dominic seeks Anita's help with Sabin's decay and studies the unusual power connecting Anita, Jean-Claude, and Richard.
characters.name: Dominic Dumare

characters.description: The established leader of the St. Louis werewolf pack. Marcus treats Richard's refusal to submit or issue a lethal challenge as a weakness that can be used to preserve the existing order.
characters.name: Marcus Fletcher

characters.description: Marcus's partner and a dominant power within the pack. Raina uses fear, loyalty, and personal coercion to maintain her influence over wolves who lack the strength to oppose her.
characters.name: Raina Wallis

characters.description: The leader of St. Louis's wereleopards and an ally of Raina. Gabriel participates in the shapeshifter coalition surrounding Marcus and regards less powerful people as resources for those able to dominate them.
characters.name: Gabriel

characters.description: A young werewolf caught between Richard's reforming ambitions and the authority of Marcus and Raina. Stephen's vulnerability gives Anita and Richard a personal reason to confront abuses that pack custom has allowed.
characters.name: Stephen

characters.description: A young werewolf who works for Jean-Claude and acts as a willing source of blood. Jason moves between the vampire and werewolf communities, helping Anita understand when the two hierarchies are cooperating and when they are using one another.
characters.name: Jason Schuyler

characters.description: A highly capable contract killer pursuing the bounty on Anita. Harley combines patience with specialized preparation and is dangerous enough that Edward treats him as a professional equal rather than an ordinary gunman.
characters.name: Harley

recaps.ending: Richard finally challenges Marcus and kills him, becoming leader of the St. Louis werewolf pack. The victory also forces Anita to witness the part of Richard's nature that he has tried to keep separate from their relationship, and her reaction breaks the confidence on which their engagement depended. Raina and Gabriel are killed after their coercion of weaker shapeshifters turns into a direct attack, ending their control over the local wolves and leopards. Cassandra and Dominic are exposed as serving a hidden plan centered on Sabin and the power shared by Anita, Jean-Claude, and Richard; they turn on Anita and are killed when the plan fails. The professional killers pursuing Anita are also defeated, with Edward instrumental in ending the contract threat. During the converging conflicts, Anita, Jean-Claude, and Richard form a powerful metaphysical triumvirate. After recoiling from Richard's transformation and killing of Marcus, Anita goes to Jean-Claude and becomes his lover. She ends her engagement to Richard. Richard remains linked to both of them through the triumvirate and now leads the pack, so the emotional triangle survives even though Anita has chosen Jean-Claude as her partner at the book's close.
recaps.in_short: Edward warns Anita Blake that a large contract has been placed on her life. As assassins close in, she is also drawn into two supernatural crises: the dying master vampire Sabin seeks help for his physical decay, and Richard must settle his challenge to Marcus for leadership of the St. Louis werewolves. Protecting vulnerable pack members brings Anita into direct conflict with Marcus, Raina, and Gabriel. The pressures on Anita, Richard, and Jean-Claude create a metaphysical triumvirate that shares their power. Richard kills Marcus and becomes pack leader, while Raina and Gabriel are killed when their abuses lead to a final confrontation. Cassandra and the necromancer Dominic reveal a concealed agenda involving Sabin and the triumvirate, but their plan fails and they die. Edward helps eliminate the hired killers. Anita is unable to accept what she sees when Richard embraces the lethal requirements of pack leadership; she turns to Jean-Claude, becomes his lover, and ends her engagement, although Richard remains supernaturally bound to them both.

recaps.text: Previously: Anita Blake raises the dead professionally and executes vampires under court order. Jean-Claude became master vampire of St. Louis after Anita killed his predecessor and placed two mystical marks on Anita, though she refuses his claim that she is his human servant. Anita fell in love with Richard Zeeman, a werewolf science teacher, while Jean-Claude continued to pursue her. During an investigation into shapeshifter disappearances, Jean-Claude forced a compromise in which Anita agreed to date both men. Richard proposed and Anita accepted, but the agreement remained. On a later assignment near Branson, Anita and her trainee Larry confronted the master vampire Seraphina and a betrayal involving the ancient being Bloody Bones. Jean-Claude's intervention was essential to Anita's survival. Anita begins this book engaged to Richard but less able to dismiss her attraction and growing reliance on Jean-Claude; Richard's unresolved struggle with pack leader Marcus continues beside that romantic rivalry.

Edward warns Anita that someone has offered a substantial payment for her death and that experienced contract killers are likely to compete for it. Early attacks confirm that the threat is organized rather than a consequence of one of Anita's open police cases. Richard and Jean-Claude both want to protect her, but accepting either man's protection carries political and personal costs. Anita remains engaged to Richard while continuing the dates she promised Jean-Claude, and the attempt on her life makes it impossible to keep their rivalry separate from practical decisions about where she can safely stay and whom she can trust.

Cassandra, a capable werewolf, joins the group guarding Anita. A second problem arrives with Sabin, an ancient master vampire whose body is failing after he stopped taking human blood. His human servant, the necromancer Dominic Dumare, believes Anita's unusual affinity with the dead may offer a cure. Jean-Claude has reasons to help another master while also fearing what Sabin's condition might imply for vampires who deny their nature. Anita agrees to investigate without promising that her power can reverse the damage. The assassins remain active, forcing every meeting to take place under heightened security.

The conflict within Richard's pack becomes as urgent as the contract on Anita. Marcus and Raina maintain control through dominance and intimidation, supported by Gabriel's wereleopards. Stephen and other less powerful shapeshifters pay the price for that arrangement. Richard has the strength to challenge Marcus and wants to reform the pack, but he still resists the requirement that a leadership challenge end in death. Anita's interventions make her a participant in the dispute even though she is not a werewolf. Cassandra appears to offer protection outside the most compromised local loyalties, while Dominic continues studying the power around Anita and Jean-Claude.

Professional killers continue testing Anita's defenses, and Edward helps turn their methods against them. Harley emerges as the most dangerous of the remaining assassins. At the same time, Anita's defense of Stephen and her refusal to tolerate Raina and Gabriel's coercion make a peaceful settlement with the shapeshifter leadership impossible. Richard must either accept Marcus's authority or issue the challenge he has delayed. Jean-Claude argues that Richard cannot claim leadership while rejecting every part of werewolf law, a judgment that also sharpens their contest over Anita. The supernatural connection among the three grows stronger under repeated danger.

The assassin threat, Sabin's request, and the pack struggle converge. Anita and Edward narrow the field of contract killers, but the source of the bounty and the supernatural interests surrounding it remain entangled. Richard accepts that Marcus will not yield and prepares for a formal challenge. Anita, Jean-Claude, and Richard discover that their existing ties can combine into a triumvirate, amplifying their abilities and making each vulnerable to the others. Raina and Gabriel respond to the loss of control over weaker shapeshifters with direct violence. Cassandra and Dominic remain close to the group as the final confrontations approach, apparently committed to protecting Anita and finding a way to stabilize Sabin.

Richard fights and kills Marcus, taking control of the St. Louis pack. Anita sees him fully accept the violent reality of the challenge, and the experience destroys her belief that she can marry him while keeping his werewolf nature at a distance. Raina and Gabriel are killed after their campaign of coercion becomes a direct attack. Cassandra and Dominic then reveal that their loyalty has been to a concealed plan involving Sabin and the power of the new triumvirate. They turn against Anita, Jean-Claude, and Richard but are defeated and killed. Edward helps dispose of the remaining professional killers, ending the immediate contract threat. Anita, Richard, and Jean-Claude survive with their metaphysical triumvirate intact. Anita goes to Jean-Claude, becomes his lover, and ends her engagement to Richard. Richard is now pack leader and remains supernaturally joined to both of them, leaving the former romantic contest transformed rather than fully resolved.

characters.description: Once the most famous Diviner in America, now a wanted fugitive with her face in every newspaper for a disaster she did not cause. She is grieving Mabel, furious with the adults who manufactured her, and holding the group together mostly by refusing to stop talking. Her gift for reading objects has become the group's main way of finding out anything true.
characters.name: Evie O'Neill

characters.description: The pickpocket who can keep from being seen, on the run with the others and carrying his own grief and the unfinished business of his mother. Practical about hiding, feeding and moving a group of hunted people, and in love with Evie at the worst possible moment.
characters.name: Sam Lloyd

characters.description: The Follies star who can call fire, now unable to go back to the stage that made her recognisable. Her control has been shaken badly by everything that happened in New York, and she is afraid of what her own gift does when she is frightened.
characters.name: Theta Knight

characters.description: The Harlem healer and poet, a fugitive travelling with his younger brother through a country where being Black and wanted is doubly dangerous. His healing costs him more each time he uses it, and he is trying to keep Isaiah out of a fight the boy insists on joining.
characters.name: Memphis Campbell

characters.description: Memphis's younger brother, whose visions now arrive constantly and reach across the whole country. He is the one the dead and the dreaming find easiest to reach, which makes him the group's best source of warning and the most exposed person in it.
characters.name: Isaiah Campbell

characters.description: The Chinatown dream walker, who can find and speak with the dead in dreams, travelling with the group and applying the same hard scepticism to every plan they make. She is the one who asks what the evidence actually shows.
characters.name: Ling Chan

characters.description: The dream walker and songwriter, whose ability to reach sleepers across great distances becomes the group's telegraph now that they are scattered. Steady company in bad conditions, and increasingly worn down by how much of the work falls on his gift.
characters.name: Henry DuBois

characters.description: Will's assistant, unnaturally strong and dependent on a serum manufactured by the man now hunting them. Every day on the road takes him further from a supply he cannot live without, and he knows exactly who controls it.
characters.name: Jericho Jones

characters.description: The blind singer who once drained Isaiah nearly to death and was himself a subject of the wartime programme. He travels with the Campbell brothers now, trying to be worth the trust he was given back, and he knows things about the programme nobody else living does.
characters.name: Bill Johnson

characters.description: Evie's uncle, who confessed his part in manufacturing the Diviners far too late to be forgiven for it. He is still the best scholar of the thing they are fighting, and he is trying to be useful to young people who no longer trust him.
characters.name: Will Fitzgerald

characters.description: Will's former colleague on the wartime programme, who spent years tracking the children it produced and warning about what was opened at Hopeful Harbor. Clear-eyed about her own guilt and unwilling to waste time on it.
characters.name: Sister Walker

characters.description: The industrialist who funded the programme that made the Diviners, opened the breach with his machine, and then handed the blame to them. He still intends to deliver the future he promised the country, and he has the government, the press and a great deal of money behind him.
characters.name: Jake Marlowe

characters.description: The man in the tall stovepipe hat, attended by crows, who raises the dead and walks between the living world and the place beyond the breach. He is unfailingly polite, enjoys an audience, and deals in bargains that cost more than they appear to. The dead now rise wherever he has been.
characters.name: The King of Crows

characters.description: The elderly woman from the Bennington who knew what walked at night long before anyone believed her, and who once helped bind a man the King of Crows had remade. What she remembers about him is older and more specific than anything in Will's collection.
characters.name: Adelaide Proctor

characters.description: A young Diviner living on a farm far out in the middle of the country, who reaches the others in dreams and says she has seen how the King of Crows can be stopped. Isolated, watched over by her family, and very certain about what has to happen next.
characters.name: Sarah Beth Olson

recaps.text: Previously: Evie O'Neill, who reads the past of any object she touches, came to New York in 1926, helped destroy the spirit of the cult leader John Hobbes, and became famous as a Diviner. She gathered a circle of others with manufactured gifts: the unseen pickpocket Sam Lloyd, the fire-caller Theta Knight, the dream walkers Henry DuBois and Ling Chan, the Harlem healer Memphis Campbell and his visionary brother Isaiah, and Will's assistant Jericho, kept alive by an experimental serum. The dream walkers ended a lethal sleeping sickness beneath Chinatown. Then the whole truth came out: during the war, Evie's uncle Will Fitzgerald, Sister Walker and the industrialist Jake Marlowe ran Project Buffalo, dosing pregnant women to produce Diviners, and their experiment at Hopeful Harbor tore open a door that was never shut. Through it comes the King of Crows, the man in the stovepipe hat, who raises the dead and trades in bargains. When Marlowe demonstrated his Eye machine at his exhibition of the American future, the breach opened wide, the dead poured through, and the Diviners closed it at the cost of Evie's friend Mabel Rose. Marlowe blamed the deaths on them. Hunted by the law and the newspapers, the Diviners scattered and ran, with the dead rising across the country behind them.

The Diviners are fugitives. Marlowe's account of the exhibition disaster is the official one, their faces are in the papers, and government men are looking for them, so the group breaks up and gets out of New York in pieces rather than together. The dead are no longer a New York problem: they rise in fields, towns and cemeteries across the country, and the King of Crows walks among them, unhurried and talkative, calling on the Diviners in dreams to offer terms. Evie is carrying Mabel's death and the knowledge that everything she is was engineered by her own uncle. Ghosts find her, and the ones she loved are not exempt.

The scattered group makes its way across America by whatever means will take fugitives: freight trains, sleeping cars staffed by porters willing to look away, a travelling circus, a barnstorming outfit selling flights at county fairs. Memphis and Isaiah travel with Bill Johnson, and the country they cross is dangerous to them in ways that have nothing to do with ghosts. Theta cannot use the name that made her famous. Henry's dream walking becomes the group's only reliable way of passing messages between parties hundreds of miles apart, and through it a girl none of them has met reaches Isaiah: a young Diviner on a farm far out in the middle of the country who says she knows how the King of Crows can be stopped.

Town by town, the Diviners run into the consequences of the breach: the recently buried walking, whole communities emptied out, people who will not admit what they have seen. They intervene where they can and learn how much their gifts cost when used hard and often. Evie's road takes her back to Zenith, Ohio and the family she left, which forces a reckoning with her mother and with the brother she lost to the war. Marlowe's people stay close behind them, and the King of Crows keeps appearing to each of them alone, always with an offer shaped exactly to what that person wants most.

Piece by piece the group assembles the King of Crows' own history, which is older than the war and older than Project Buffalo, and turns on a bargain he made long ago and a brother he could not keep. Understanding what he is changes what stopping him would mean. Meanwhile Marlowe has not abandoned the Eye: he is rebuilding it, bigger, with government backing, still insisting the breach is a power source rather than a door. The Diviners set out for the farm in the middle of the country where the girl from the dreams is waiting, on the strength of a plan none of them has been able to verify.

characters.description: The Banu Nahida of Daevabad and the only acknowledged Nahid healer alive, married to the emir Muntadhir and confined to a palace she is not permitted to leave. Five years after she was brought to the city she has become a formidable healer, but her position rests entirely on the king's tolerance, and she survives it the way she survived Cairo: by watching, bargaining, and giving away nothing she does not have to. She still does not know who her parents were.
characters.name: Nahri

characters.description: The king's younger son, exiled to the Geziri provinces and widely expected to die there. He survived, and in the desert village that took him in he has found a use for what the marid left in him: he can call water where there is none. He hides what that means, prays it will fade, and has built a life among people who value him for the well he found rather than the name he carries.
characters.name: Alizayd

characters.description: The Nahids' warrior, killed on Daevabad's lake and raised again by Banu Manizheh, restored to the body and the unbound magic his people held before Suleiman's punishment. He is bound to Manizheh's service and to a plan he did not choose, training soldiers in a hidden camp far from the city, and he carries the memory of everything he did the last time he was handed orders and told they were necessary.
characters.name: Dara

characters.description: The Nahid healer the world believed the ifrit murdered twenty years ago, alive and at large beyond Daevabad's veil. She raised Dara from the dead, she has the grand wazir's loyalty, and she intends to take back the city her family lost. Nahri is her daughter, a fact Nahri does not know.
characters.name: Manizheh

characters.description: King of Daevabad and bearer of Suleiman's seal. Five years on he governs by threat and hostage: he knows precisely whom each person under him loves, and he says so. He has kept Nahri obedient by naming what will happen to the Daeva tribe, and to individual Daevas, the moment she disappoints him.
characters.name: Ghassan

characters.description: Emir of Daevabad and Nahri's husband, in a marriage that is a treaty rather than a partnership. Still fonder of wine, poetry and company than of governing, he has spent five years watching his father use his wife as an instrument, unable to protect her, his brother, or Jamshid e-Pramukh, whose injuries have never healed.
characters.name: Muntadhir

characters.description: Ghassan's daughter and the most politically capable of his children, who has spent her younger brother's exile managing the household, the court's expectations and the family's public face.
characters.name: Zaynab

characters.description: Grand wazir of Daevabad and Jamshid's father, the senior Daeva in the king's government and an unwavering advocate for what he believes his tribe is owed. He travels frequently to the Daeva provinces on the crown's business.
characters.name: Kaveh

characters.description: Kaveh's son and Muntadhir's closest companion, left partly crippled by the Afshin's arrows five years ago. No healer, Nahri included, has been able to undo the damage, and he has rebuilt a life around the limits it set.
characters.name: Jamshid

characters.description: Nahri's assistant in the palace infirmary, a Daeva woman who trained under the previous Nahids and has guided Nahri's practice since she arrived. Devoted to Daeva tradition and to the restoration of her tribe's standing, she is the closest thing Nahri has to a teacher.
characters.name: Nisreen

characters.description: A Geziri djinn of Bir Nabat, the desert village that took Ali in after finding him half-dead. Talkative, cheerful and hard to offend, he has become Ali's closest friend and treats the prince's grim self-denial as a personal challenge.
characters.name: Lubayd

characters.description: A Geziri warrior of Bir Nabat, blunt and formidably capable, who fights beside Ali and has no patience at all for the politics of Daevabad.
characters.name: Aqisa

characters.description: An ifrit who has attached himself to Manizheh's cause. Like all his kind he is one of the original daevas who refused Suleiman's judgement, unchanged and very old, and his knowledge of what the Nahids used to be able to do is worth more to Manizheh than his sword. Nothing he offers is offered freely.
characters.name: Aeshma

characters.description: Ali's mother, an Ayaanle noblewoman of Ta Ntry and Ghassan's queen, who returns to Daevabad with plans of her own. Wealthy, exceptionally well connected and entirely unsentimental about court politics, she has never accepted her son's exile and does not intend to leave his future to his father.
characters.name: Hatset

characters.description: A shafit physician in Daevabad, trained in human medicine, who treats the part-human patients the Nahid infirmary will not admit. Capable and direct, she is deeply suspicious of any offer of partnership from a Nahid, and says so.
characters.name: Subhashini

recaps.ending: Manizheh's assault succeeds completely. Dara brings her forces across the cursed lake and destroys the Citadel, killing most of the Royal Guard with it, while inside the palace Kaveh releases a vapour Manizheh built from Nahid poison-craft: it kills Geziri djinn and leaves everyone else untouched. The Navasatem gathering becomes a massacre. Ghassan dies with the rest, and Muntadhir is left mortally wounded and beyond ordinary healing. Suleiman's seal passes to Alizayd, who survives the vapour only because of the marid magic in him. Kaveh reveals that Jamshid is his son by Manizheh, which makes Jamshid a Nahid and Nahri's half-brother, and Manizheh tells Nahri to her face that she is her daughter. Refusing to be taken, Nahri and Ali throw themselves into the lake and are carried half a world away, surfacing in the Nile. Because the bearer of Suleiman's seal is no longer on the island, Daevabad's magic goes out with him: the wards, the conjuring, the healing, all of it. Manizheh ends the book holding a city that no longer works, keeping Muntadhir alive as leverage over Jamshid, whom she means to install as her heir. Dara has delivered exactly what he was raised from the dead to deliver, and is beginning to understand what he has let himself become for a second time. Nahri and Ali are alive, magicless and stranded in Egypt, and they are the only two people who might undo any of it.
recaps.in_short: Five years after The City of Brass, Nahri is Daevabad's Banu Nahida and Muntadhir's unwilling wife, kept obedient by King Ghassan's threats against her tribe. Ali, exiled to the desert, has survived assassins and hidden the water magic the marid left in him. Summoned home for Navasatem, the celebration held once a century, he joins Nahri in rebuilding the ruined Nahid hospital to treat the city's despised shafit. While treating Jamshid, Nahri discovers he carries Nahid blood. Outside the city, Dara, resurrected and bound to Banu Manizheh, trains her army while arguing against her methods. Manizheh strikes during Navasatem: Dara destroys the Citadel while Kaveh releases a poison that kills Daevabad's Geziri, Ghassan among them. Muntadhir is mortally wounded, Kaveh reveals Jamshid as his and Manizheh's son, and Nahri learns that Manizheh is her mother. Suleiman's seal passes to Ali, and when he and Nahri escape into the lake and surface in the Nile, Daevabad's magic fails with the seal-bearer gone. Manizheh holds a broken city; Nahri and Ali are stranded in Egypt.

recaps.text: Previously, in The City of Brass: Nahri, a young con artist in Ottoman Cairo, accidentally summoned Darayavahoush the Afshin, a daeva warrior, and learned that she carried the blood of the Nahids, the family of magical healers who once ruled the djinn city of Daevabad. Dara brought her there, hunted by ifrit the whole way. Daevabad had been taken from the Nahids fourteen centuries earlier by the Qahtani family, who rule its six tribes and confine the part-human shafit to poverty. King Ghassan installed Nahri in his palace as the first Nahid healer in twenty years and set his devout younger son Alizayd to tutor her; the two became friends while Ali was secretly funding a shafit organization, a betrayal that cost lives and destroyed his standing. Nahri learned that Dara is remembered by the other tribes as the Scourge of Qui-zi, responsible for a massacre of shafit during the war, and she bargained a betrothal to Ghassan's heir Muntadhir to protect herself and the Daeva tribe. When Dara tried to take her out of the city, the escape became a bloodbath: he crippled Jamshid e-Pramukh with his arrows, and on the cursed lake the marid seized Ali, possessed him and used him to kill Dara. Nahri was married to Muntadhir; Ali was exiled to the Geziri desert on an assignment meant to kill him. In the epilogue Dara woke restored to life and to the unbound magic his people held before Suleiman's punishment, raised by Kaveh e-Pramukh and by Banu Manizheh, the Nahid healer believed murdered two decades ago, who revealed that Nahri is her daughter.

Five years have passed. Nahri is Daevabad's Banu Nahida and Muntadhir's wife in a marriage neither of them chose, running the palace infirmary and effectively a prisoner of Ghassan's goodwill. Ali survived his exile: after assassins came for him in Am Gezira, the desert village of Bir Nabat took him in, and he has quietly used the water magic the marid left in him to bring the village a spring. He refuses to think about what that magic makes him. Far from both of them, Dara is alive. Restored by Manizheh, bound to her service and to a body whose power he does not recognize, he is training a small force of young Daeva recruits in a hidden camp, and he is beginning to understand that the woman who raised him from the dead intends to take Daevabad back by any means she can reach.

Ghassan summons Ali home to Daevabad for Navasatem, the festival held once a century, and everyone involved reads the summons as a trap of some kind. Ali returns with his Bir Nabat friends Lubayd and Aqisa to a court that has not forgiven him: Muntadhir treats his brother's return as a threat to his own position, and their mother Hatset arrives from Ta Ntry with plans for her son that he has not agreed to. Nahri, denied any authority beyond the infirmary, has an ambition of her own. She wants to reopen the ruined Nahid hospital in the shafit district and treat shafit patients in it, which would break with everything her tribe expects of her and everything Ghassan is willing to permit.

Nahri and Ali resume the alliance that got them both into trouble five years ago, working together on the hospital. She recruits shafit physicians, among them Subhashini Sen, who has no reason to trust a Nahid, and finds that rebuilding the place means confronting what her own family did to the shafit long before the Qahtanis ever arrived. Ghassan permits the project because it is useful to him, and goes on controlling Nahri by naming exactly who will suffer if she disappoints him. Muntadhir watches his wife and his brother work together and draws his own conclusions. In the mountains, Dara's misgivings harden as he learns what Manizheh is prepared to use: ifrit allies, and Nahid craft turned to purposes no healer should be putting it to.

Treating Jamshid, Nahri finds something that should not be there: his body resists her healing the way only Nahid flesh does. Jamshid, the grand wazir's son, carries Nahid blood, and the implications go far beyond a medical curiosity, because a second living Nahid changes who can hold Daevabad and who can be forced to. Kaveh's behaviour, and his long absences to the Daeva provinces, start to look like something other than provincial administration. Ali's questions about where the treasury's money has been going lead him toward the same answer from a different direction. Preparations for Navasatem fill the city with visitors and soldiers, and violence between shafit and Daeva becomes an almost daily occurrence.

The hospital opens, and for a short while it works: shafit and Daeva treated in the same building, with Nahri, Ali and Subhashini's physicians sharing the wards. It does not survive the city's politics. Navasatem brings the tribes together and brings every grievance between them along too; bloodshed between shafit and Daeva escalates, and Ghassan's answer is to tighten his hold on everyone who might matter, Nahri included. She and Muntadhir reach a fragile understanding and then lose it. Kaveh departs for the provinces at a conspicuously convenient moment, and beyond the veil Manizheh's preparations are complete.

In the last days of Navasatem, Ghassan's grip closes. He forces Nahri into a position with no acceptable answer, and Ali, whose marid-given abilities can no longer be hidden from his father, becomes a liability the king will not tolerate. Muntadhir is left choosing between his brother, his wife and his king, and chooses badly in every direction. Beyond the lake, Manizheh's army is ready. Dara, who has spent the book arguing with her about what is genuinely necessary, is given his orders, and obeys them.

Manizheh takes Daevabad. Dara brings her army across the cursed lake and brings down the Citadel, killing most of the Royal Guard, while inside the palace Kaveh releases a vapour Manizheh made from Nahid poison-craft that kills Geziri djinn and nobody else. The Navasatem gathering becomes a massacre: Geziri die throughout the palace and the city, Ghassan among them, and Muntadhir is left mortally wounded. Suleiman's seal passes to Ali, who lives through the vapour because of what the marid did to him. Kaveh reveals that Jamshid is his son by Manizheh, making Jamshid a Nahid and Nahri's half-brother, and Nahri meets her mother for the first time and is told exactly what she is. With the palace lost and nothing left to hold, Nahri and Ali throw themselves into the lake rather than be taken. Because the bearer of the seal has left the island, Daevabad's magic goes out with him.

Nahri and Ali surface half a world away, in the Nile, alive and stranded with no magic to carry them anywhere. Behind them, Daevabad belongs to Banu Manizheh: a city without magic, its Geziri population devastated, its Royal Guard destroyed, Muntadhir dying and kept as leverage, and Jamshid claimed as the Nahid heir his mother intends to seat on the throne. Dara has won everything he was raised from the dead to win, and understands too late what it cost and who paid.

characters.description: A full Ranger serving Araluen, now experienced in both covert investigation and open conflict. Will accompanies Halt into Hibernia to scout a growing religious movement whose public claims conceal organised intimidation.
characters.name: Will

characters.description: One of Araluen's most famous Rangers and Will's former mentor. Halt is usually guarded about his origins, but the mission to Clonmel takes him back to the Hibernian royal family and a history he has kept from almost everyone.
characters.name: Halt

characters.description: Will and Halt's closest warrior ally, an exceptional knight whose honesty and fighting reputation make him well suited to a public role in their campaign against the Outsiders.
characters.name: Horace Altman

characters.description: Commandant of the Ranger Corps and Halt's old friend. Crowley identifies the Outsiders' spread through Hibernia as a threat likely to reach Araluen and sends a small team to learn how the movement works.
characters.name: Crowley

characters.description: A skilled Courier and Will's partner. Alyss remains in Araluen while the Rangers leave for Hibernia, part of the life and personal future to which Will expects to return after the mission.
characters.name: Alyss Mainwaring

characters.description: A gifted cook and Horace's childhood friend at Redmont. Jenny's warmth toward Horace makes the normally composed knight noticeably uncertain before he leaves on the Hibernian mission.
characters.name: Jenny Dalby

characters.description: Will's Ranger horse, trained to respond to quiet signals and to move safely through difficult country. Tug remains essential to Will's scouting as the group crosses Hibernia.
characters.name: Tug

characters.description: The charismatic leader of the Outsiders. Tennyson promises divine protection to frightened communities in return for wealth and obedience, presenting each expansion of his following as proof of spiritual power.
characters.name: Tennyson

characters.description: The followers and enforcers of Tennyson's movement. They enter districts suffering from raids and disorder, then demand payment and allegiance in exchange for the protection their leader claims to provide.
characters.name: The Outsiders

characters.description: King of Clonmel and Halt's twin brother. Ferris resembles Halt closely but has governed through avoidance and self-interest, allowing royal authority to weaken while the Outsiders gain influence.
characters.name: King Ferris

characters.description: Ferris's nephew and heir, a young Hibernian noble who takes the danger to Clonmel more seriously than his uncle does. Sean is prepared to support the Araluens' effort to restore confidence in lawful rule.
characters.name: Sean Carrick

characters.description: A professional assassin from Genovesa employed by Tennyson. Bacari relies on concealment, poison and the small crossbow associated with his trade rather than meeting enemies openly.
characters.name: Bacari

characters.description: One of the Genovesan killers serving Tennyson. Marisi works from hiding and helps turn carefully planned violence into apparent evidence of the Outsiders' supernatural favour.
characters.name: Marisi

recaps.ending: The Rangers expose the machinery behind Tennyson's power in Clonmel: the Outsiders help create the insecurity they promise to cure, while hidden Genovesan crossbowmen turn murder into apparent divine judgement. Will counters the concealed assassins and Horace's public courage gives the people a visible alternative to fear. King Ferris does not live to repair the weakness that enabled the movement; he is killed during the crisis. Because Halt is his twin, Halt briefly takes Ferris's place long enough to prevent immediate collapse and secure the succession for their nephew Sean Carrick. Sean becomes king with a chance to rebuild Clonmel's authority. Tennyson nevertheless escapes with surviving followers and Genovesan killers, so the organisation has been checked rather than destroyed. Will, Halt and Horace pursue him beyond Clonmel. The book therefore ends with the kingdom saved but its antagonist still at large, opening the Tennyson and Genovesan arc continued in Halt's Peril.
recaps.in_short: Crowley sends Will, Halt and Horace to Hibernia, where a sect called the Outsiders is exploiting weak kingdoms. Its leader Tennyson secretly benefits from raids and disorder, then demands gold and obedience for promised protection. In Clonmel, Halt reveals that the ineffective King Ferris is his twin brother and that Halt himself has a claim to the throne he left behind. The companions try to restore confidence in lawful rule: Horace becomes a conspicuous champion while Will investigates the tricks behind Tennyson's supposed miracles. Hidden Genovesan assassins, including Bacari and Marisi, use crossbow bolts and poison to make the sect's enemies appear struck down by divine power. The deception is exposed, but Ferris is killed. Halt impersonates his identical brother just long enough to steady the kingdom and place their nephew Sean Carrick on the throne. Tennyson escapes with the remaining assassins, and the three Araluens pursue him into the next book.

recaps.text: Previously: Will trained under Halt in the Ranger Corps, helped defeat Morgarath and survived captivity in Skandia with Princess Cassandra. Will, Halt and Horace later helped Skandia defeat a Temujai invasion and returned home as allies of their former enemies. Before Will's apprenticeship ended, the friends also travelled to Arrida to free Erak from a ransom conspiracy; Will's performance there helped prove he was ready for the silver oakleaf. As a full Ranger he protected Seacliff, then went undercover at Castle Macindaw with the Courier Alyss. They uncovered Keren's plan to poison the ruling family and hand the northern fortress to Scotti invaders. With Horace, the healer Malcolm and a Skandian crew, Will retook Macindaw and rescued Alyss. Will and Alyss acknowledged their love. Will is now an established Ranger, while Halt and Horace remain the partners he trusts most on dangerous missions.

At Redmont, Will, Halt and Horace are drawn away from ordinary fief life by a Ranger Corps concern. Reports from Hibernia describe the spread of the Outsiders, a religious movement that enters districts already suffering raids and lawlessness. Its priests promise safety in exchange for donations and loyalty, weakening rulers who cannot provide the same protection. Crowley believes the method could spread beyond Hibernia if it succeeds there. He sends the three friends to investigate quietly and help the threatened kingdom of Clonmel before the movement becomes too deeply established.

Travelling through Hibernia, the Araluens see how the Outsiders create loyalty. Tennyson is a commanding speaker who arrives among frightened people with confident promises, while armed followers make his protection seem practical as well as spiritual. Evidence suggests that the disorder assisting the movement is not accidental: communities are pressured by attacks and then offered relief on Tennyson's terms. Will gathers information discreetly, Horace provides visible strength, and Halt guides them toward Clonmel, where the weakness of the crown has made the kingdom especially vulnerable.

In Clonmel, Halt reveals the personal history behind his knowledge of the country. King Ferris is his identical twin brother. Halt left Hibernia after a struggle over the succession and built his life in Araluen, while Ferris took the throne. Ferris has become an evasive ruler whose subjects no longer trust him to protect them, giving Tennyson room to present the Outsiders as a stronger authority.
